anchor: Out of the cradle endlessly rocking
title: Title, publication and revision
short: First printed as 'A Child's Reminiscence' (1859), retitled 'A Word Out of the Sea' (1860), and given its present title in 1871.
body: The poem first appeared on the front page of the New York Saturday Press on 24 December 1859 as 'A Child's Reminiscence', with an editorial note, probably by Whitman, presenting it as a holiday gift. The Cincinnati Daily Commercial attacked it as drivel, and the Saturday Press replied on 7 January 1860 with 'All About a Mocking-Bird', a defence that Whitman himself may have written. It entered the 1860 Leaves of Grass as 'A Word Out of the Sea', was revised in 1867, took its present title in 1871, and reached its final form in 1881, when it opened the 'Sea-Drift' cluster. The archive text is this late version. The opening line itself sets the frame: the sea is a cradle endlessly rocking, and the cradle returns at the close with the old crone, linking birth and death.

title: The overture: one long periodic sentence
short: The first 22 lines form a single sentence whose main verb comes only at the end: 'A reminiscence sing.'
body: Whitman opens with a cascade of prepositional phrases ('Out of', 'Over', 'Down from', 'Up from', 'From') that pile up the sources of the poem, the rocking sea, the bird's throat, the September midnight, the memories, before the subject 'I' and the verb 'sing' arrive in l. 22. Leo Spitzer's classic explication analyses this sentence in detail as a deliberate rhetorical period, and the structure has often been compared to an operatic overture that announces the themes developed later. The delay enacts the poem's subject, the slow gathering of memory into song. The anaphora (repeated openings) is typical of Whitman's free verse, which borrows from the parallelism of the King James Bible.

title: the musical shuttle
short: The bird's throat is a weaver's shuttle, darting to and fro and weaving song as a shuttle weaves cloth.
body: A shuttle carries the weft thread back and forth across a loom. The metaphor captures the rapid, repeated phrases of the mockingbird's song and the bird's darting flight 'to and fro', and it makes song a kind of weaving, in which separate notes are woven into a fabric. Later the boy 'translates' the notes, and the poem itself weaves together bird, sea, boy and man.

title: Ninth-month; Fifth-month
short: September and May: Whitman uses the Quaker numbered names for months, avoiding the 'pagan' month names.
body: The Society of Friends (Quakers) traditionally avoided the names of months and weekdays derived from Roman and Norse gods, calling them by number: First-day for Sunday, Fifth-month for May, Ninth-month for September. Whitman's mother came from a family with Quaker connections, and he admired the Quaker preacher Elias Hicks. The usage gives the poem a plain, homely, Long Island idiom. The two months mark the story's span: the birds nest in May ('Fifth-month grass'), and the song the boy hears on the beach is remembered from a Ninth-month (September) midnight, as summer ends.

sources.cite: Harold W. Blodgett and Sculley Bradley, eds., Leaves of Grass: Comprehensive Reader's Edition (New York: New York UP, 1965), notes to 'Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking'
Walt Whitman, 'Elias Hicks', in November Boughs (1888)

title: sad brother
short: The bereaved mockingbird, whom the boy recognises as a brother in suffering and later in song.
body: The poet addresses the bird directly as a 'brother', and the word recurs ('Yes my brother I know', 'Following you my brother', 'my dusky demon and brother'). The kinship is double: the boy shares the bird's grief, and he will inherit its vocation as a singer. Romantic poets had made birds into figures of the poet (Shelley's skylark, Keats's nightingale), but Whitman's bird is a fellow mourner rather than an immortal voice above human sorrow.

title: 'I, chanter of pains and joys'
short: The adult poet, weeping like a boy again on the shore, introduces himself as a singer who joins 'here and hereafter'.
body: The lines set up the poem's double time: the man ('yet by these tears a little boy again') throws himself on the sand and recalls the childhood scene. He calls himself 'chanter of pains and joys, uniter of here and hereafter', which anticipates the end, where the sea's word death unites life and what follows it. 'Taking all hints to use them, but swiftly leaping beyond them' is a statement of Whitman's poetics, using experience as a starting point for vision. Stephen Whicher argued that the tears belong to the adult Whitman of 1859, in a personal crisis, more than to the child.

title: Paumanok
short: The Native American name for Long Island, Whitman's birthplace, which he used throughout Leaves of Grass.
body: Whitman was born at West Hills, Long Island, in 1819, and spent much of his childhood and youth on the island. He preferred the Algonquian name 'Paumanok', which he understood to mean something like 'fish-shaped', to the English one, and it appears throughout Leaves of Grass ('Starting from fish-shape Paumanok where I was born', 'Starting from Paumanok'). Here 'Once Paumanok' begins the story itself, as though the island were the poem's 'once upon a time'. The poem's seashore, briers and sand belong to the island's north and south shores, which Whitman knew well.

title: two feather'd guests from Alabama
short: A pair of mockingbirds, unusual so far north, visiting Long Island from the South to nest.
body: The northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos) was then chiefly a southern bird, and a nesting pair on Long Island would have been a notable sight. Calling them 'guests from Alabama' makes them visitors from far away, and in 1859, on the eve of the Civil War, the southern origin may carry a faint resonance of national division and union ('two together'). The mockingbird is famous for its loud, varied song, often sung at night, which makes it a natural figure for the poet.

title: 'Cautiously peering, absorbing, translating'
short: The boy as the poet in embryo: watching, taking in, and turning the bird's song into human words.
body: The three participles sum up Whitman's account of how a poet is made: by attention, absorption and translation. The word recurs at l. 69 ('now translating the notes'), and the bird's arias that follow are presented as the boy's translation of birdsong into English. This makes the poem about its own origin, the moment when a child became a singer. Critics such as Spitzer read the whole poem as a myth of the poet's vocation.

title: The first aria: 'Shine! shine! shine!'
short: The bird's song of happy union, set off as a separate lyric (italic in Whitman's editions), with short rhythmic lines.
body: In Whitman's own editions the birds' songs are printed in italic, like arias set within the recitative of the narrative. The first is a duet of the two birds, happy in the sun, with the refrain 'two together' and short, strongly rhythmic lines; their steady pulse contrasts with the long narrative lines around it. Robert Faner traced the poem's alternation of recitative and aria to Whitman's passion for Italian opera, which he attended frequently in New York in the 1840s and 1850s. The triple exclamation becomes the pattern for every later aria: 'Blow! blow! blow!', 'Soothe! soothe! soothe!', 'Loud! loud! loud!'

title: 'Blow! blow! blow!'
short: After the she-bird vanishes, the he-bird's short, desperate song calls on the sea-winds to bring her back.
body: The she-bird disappears without explanation ('May-be kill'd, unknown to her mate'), a death the poem never describes, which is part of its power. The he-bird's three-line song begins the series of laments. It echoes, perhaps deliberately, the refrains of Shakespeare ('Blow, blow, thou winter wind') and of ballads, but its plainness belongs to Whitman. From now on the bird sings by night, 'on the prong of a moss-scallop'd stake', amid the slapping waves.

title: The great aria (ll. 71-129)
short: The longest song, the bird's lament for its lost mate, moves through hope, delusion and despair.
body: This sixty-line aria is the centre of the poem. The bird calls on the waves, the moon, the land, the stars and its own throat; it mistakes a dark spot in the moon and a black thing in the breakers for its mate; it hushes, thinking it hears an answer; and it ends in 'O darkness! O in vain!' and 'We two together no more'. The emotional curve follows the shape of an operatic lament, and the bird's mistakes (wind, spray, shadows of leaves) show love projecting its object onto nature. Note the moon 'heavy with love' and the sea that 'pushes upon the land, / With love': for the grieving bird, all nature is love and loss.

title: 'The aria sinking': the trio
short: As the song ends, a long catalogue gathers bird, sea and boy into a 'trio', each uttering.
body: The word 'aria' (Italian, an 'air', a solo song in opera) is Whitman's open acknowledgement of his operatic model. After the song stops, a single sentence of participles ('continuing', 'shining', 'blowing', 'moaning') gathers the whole scene: stars, winds, the moaning sea, the drooping moon, and the boy 'ecstatic', with the love in his heart 'now at last tumultuously bursting'. 'The colloquy there, the trio, each uttering' names the three voices as in an operatic ensemble: the bird's song, the sea's undertone, and the boy's soul. The bird's grief has become the boy's awakening.

sources.cite: Robert D. Faner, Walt Whitman and Opera (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1951)

title: the fierce old mother
short: The sea as an ancient mother, moaning and crying, the source of life and of the final word.
body: The sea is first a rocking cradle, then 'the fierce old mother incessantly moaning' and 'the savage old mother incessantly crying', and finally the 'old crone'. Whitman's mother-sea draws on a long tradition (life emerging from the sea; the sea as mother in many mythologies) and on his own feeling for his mother. Whicher noted that Whitman's own mother figure and the sea of death are fused here. The sea's 'undertone', its 'drown'd secret hissing', prepares the word it will finally whisper.

sources.cite: Stephen E. Whicher, 'Whitman's Awakening to Death: Toward a Biographical Reading of "Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking"', in R. W. B. Lewis, ed., The Presence of Walt Whitman (New York: Columbia UP, 1962)

title: the outsetting bard
short: The boy as a poet setting out on his career; 'outsetting' is Whitman's coinage for 'just beginning'.
body: 'Outsetting' (setting out, at the start of a journey) is an uncommon form built on 'outset', in keeping with Whitman's fondness for unusual coinages. The boy is now named a 'bard', the old Celtic title of the poet-singer that Whitman often uses for himself. The phrase marks the climax of the poem's myth of vocation: the child has become, in an instant, the poet he will be.

title: Demon or bird!
short: The boy's soul asks whether the bird is a mere bird or a 'demon', a spirit (Greek daimon) sent to awaken him.
body: The echo of Poe's 'The Raven' ('Prophet!' said I, 'thing of evil! prophet still, if bird or devil!') is often noted, and Whitman may be deliberately answering Poe: his bird is not evil but a daimon in the Greek sense, a guiding spirit or genius, like the daimonion of Socrates. Later the poet calls it 'my dusky demon and brother'. The question 'Is it indeed toward your mate you sing? or is it really to me?' is the turning point, for the boy recognises that the song is meant for him, as a call to his own vocation.

title: 'Now in a moment I know what I am for'
short: The moment of awakening: the bird's song releases 'a thousand singers' within the boy, and his peaceful childhood ends.
body: The boy, 'my tongue's use sleeping', now 'awakes' to his purpose: to sing. The bird's sorrow becomes the source of 'a thousand warbling echoes' within him, songs 'more sorrowful' than the bird's. The lines are both triumphant and fearful: 'never more shall I escape'; never again will he be 'the peaceful child I was'. 'The messenger there arous'd' may echo the Greek angelos (messenger, angel), and 'the fire, the sweet hell within' names a passion at once creative and painful, 'the unknown want'. Whicher read this as Whitman's confession of an adult crisis of 1859, projected back into childhood.

title: the fire, the sweet hell within
short: An oxymoron for the poet's newly aroused desire: a burning, painful longing that is also delicious.
body: 'Sweet hell' combines pleasure and torment in the manner of Petrarchan love poetry, where love is a sweet fire. Here the fire is the poet's vocation as well as unsatisfied love ('the cries of unsatisfied love'). The phrase is one of several in the poem that bind delight and death ('the low and delicious word death'). The oxymoron is the poem's emotional key.

title: the clue
short: The thread or key to the mystery; the boy asks for the word that will explain love and loss.
body: 'Clue' (from 'clew', a ball of thread) originally meant the thread by which Theseus found his way out of the Cretan labyrinth, and then any key to a mystery. The boy demands 'the word final, superior to all', and the poem's suspense hangs on what it will be. The sea's answer, death, is the clue: the meaning of the bird's loss and the source of all the boy's future songs.

title: the word death
short: The sea answers the boy by whispering 'death', which becomes the key to his songs; critics differ on whether it consoles.
body: The sea, 'delaying not, hurrying not', whispers 'death, death, death, death, death', the hissing sound of the surf on the sand. For Whitman the word is 'delicious', 'the word of the sweetest song and all songs'. Leo Spitzer read the ending as a consoling vision in which death is the mother who completes the cycle begun with the cradle, and poetry the reconciliation of love and death. Stephen Whicher saw instead a darker poem of crisis, in which the poet faces loss and the limits of his earlier, buoyant faith. Readers also compare Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale', where the poet is 'half in love with easeful Death'.

sources.cite: Leo Spitzer, 'Explication de Texte Applied to Walt Whitman's Poem "Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking"', in Essays on English and American Literature (Princeton: Princeton UP, 1962)

title: 'But fuse the song of my dusky demon and brother'
short: The poet's songs fuse three sources: the bird's lament, his own answering songs, and the sea's word.
body: The closing sentence says that the poet will 'fuse' the bird's song with 'the thousand responsive songs' that awoke in him that night and with 'the key, the word up from the waves'. It is Whitman's statement of how his poetry is made: from grief (the bird), from the imagination it arouses (his own songs) and from death (the sea). The poem ends quietly, 'The sea whisper'd me', where 'me' is both indirect object (whispered to me) and perhaps direct object, as if the sea whispered the poet into being.

sources.cite: Leo Spitzer, 'Explication de Texte Applied to Walt Whitman's Poem "Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking"', in Essays on English and American Literature (Princeton: Princeton UP, 1962)
Harold W. Blodgett and Sculley Bradley, eds., Leaves of Grass: Comprehensive Reader's Edition (New York: New York UP, 1965), notes to 'Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking'

title: some old crone rocking the cradle
short: The sea as an old woman rocking a cradle: the opening cradle returns, now linking birth to death.
body: The parenthesis brings the poem full circle to its first line. The sea that rocked the child's cradle now appears as an 'old crone', swathed in 'sweet garments', bending over a cradle as she whispers death. The figure suggests a grandmother or a Fate, and it makes death a nurse rather than a terror. Spitzer stressed this framing as the formal sign of the poem's reconciliation, in which death is understood as a return to the mother.
